## Tokenize


Tokenization breaks text into manageable units or tokens.  Tokenization helps preprocess text data, simplifying tasks such as filtering out punctuation, converting to lowercase, and handling special characters.  It also transforms text into numerical IDs which transformers and LLMs require. Tokenization has different methods such as spliting text into individual words,spliting words into subwords, and breaking text into individual characters.  For our model we will split our data into individual words. 

```{python}


tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("cardiffnlp/twitter-roberta-base-sentiment-latest")


```

```{python}


def tokenize(batch):
    temp = tokenizer(batch['text'], padding="max_length", truncation=True, max_length=514)
    return temp



```

## Labels

There is one last step needed to prepare our data.  As will be seen later when setting up configuation,  the model requires two variables: label2id and id2label.  As mentioned when reviewing the initial dataset, we will require a label_name and label column for creating these variables.

From the output we see the label_name and label columns. First, label2id will be created using list comprehension.  The list comprehension creates a dictionary with key/value paris.  Label_name is the key and label is the value. Basically, this is mapping label_name to label.  

 





 label2id now can be used to create id2label.   list comprehension will also be used except in the case the key/value pairs will be interchanged and the key from label2id becomes values and values become keys.  This results in id2label having label as the key and label_name as the values.

## Metrics


```{python}

precision = evaluate.load("precision")
recall = evaluate.load("recall")
f1 = evaluate.load("f1")


```

```{python}


accuracy.features

```


```{python}



def compute_metrics(eval_pred):
    predictions, labels = eval_pred
    predictions = np.argmax(predictions, axis=1)
    accuracy=accuracy.compute(predictions=predictions, references=labels)["accuracy"]
    precision=precision.compute(predictions=predictions, references=labels)["precision"]
    recall=recall.compute(predictions=predictions, references=labels)["recall"]
    f1=f1.compute(predictions=predictions, references=labels)["f1"]
    return {"accuracy":accuracy, "precision":precision, "recall":recall, "f1":f1}


```


```{python}


from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, precision_score, recall_score, f1_score




```


```{python}

def compute_metrics(pred):
    labels = pred.label_ids
    preds = pred.predictions.argmax(-1)

    acc = accuracy_score(labels, preds)
    prec = precision_score(labels, preds, average='weighted')
    rec = recall_score(labels, preds, average='weighted')
    f1 = f1_score(labels, preds, average='weighted')

    return {"accuracy": acc, "precision": prec, "recall": rec, "f1": f1}




```

```{python}
    weight_decay=0.01,
    logging_dir="./logs",
    logging_first_step=10,
    save_steps=500,
    disable_tqdm=False


)
```

The confusion matrix is a visual representation of how our model performed on predicting on the test set. It shows how many predictions were correct (TruePositives/Negatives) versus incorect (False Positives/Negatives) when compared to actual outcomes. The actual outcomes are on the x axis and the predictions are on the y axis.  If we look at negative sentiment the large number in the upper left of the matrix represents how many negative sentiment predictions were correct (true positve).  If we follow the  negative sentiment acrossthe matrix we see lower values for predicted neutral and positive sentiments. This is interpreted as the model had fewer incorrect predictions of positve or negative sentimenbt when the actual outcome was negative (false negative). Following  negative on vertically, the lower values mean the model had fewer incorrect predictions of negative sentiment when the actual outcome was neutral or positive. The model follows the same pattern for positive sentiment. The model was less accurate on neutral sentiment predictions as we see the number of false positives and false negatives  are higher as a percentage of total predictions when compared to the other sentiments. 


# Predicting on unlabled data

Now that we have our pre-trained model fine0tuned we will use it to predict on a new dataset.  The data includes New York Times comments from the 2018 year. 

```{python}

def get_prediction(text):

    input_encoded = tokenizer(text, return_tensors='pt').to(device)

    with torch.no_grad():
        outputs = model(**input_encoded)

    logits = outputs.logits

    pred = torch.argmax(logits, dim=1).item()
    return id2label[pred]


```


```{python}


def get_prediction(text):

    input_encoded = tokenizer(text, return_tensors='pt').to(device)

    with torch.no_grad():
        outputs = model(**input_encoded)

    logits = outputs.logits
    probabilities = torch.nn.functional.softmax(logits, dim=-1)

    pred = torch.argmax(probabilities, dim=-1).item()
    return probabilities, id2label[pred]



```

```{python}




def get_prediction(text):

    """
        Applies fine-tuned model and tokenizer to predict sentiment

        Args: 
            text: A string of text.

        Returns: 
            probabilites: predicted probability of each sentiment. Probabilites sum to 1.
            id2label[pred]: predicted sentiment label.
    """

    input_encoded = new_tokenizer(text, return_tensors='pt').to(device)

    with torch.no_grad():
        outputs = new_model(**input_encoded)

    logits = outputs.logits
    probabilities = torch.nn.functional.softmax(logits, dim=-1)

    pred = torch.argmax(probabilities, dim=-1).item()
    return probabilities, id2label[pred]


```


We created a function that will take in a string of text and return the probabilties of the predicted sentiments and the predicted sentiment label with the highest probabilty. Probabilty is the confidence we have in predicted label. 





For comparison, we will print the text string predicted along with the model output. 





```{python}


print(nyt_sentiments18.iloc[50,0])
get_prediction(nyt_sentiments18.iloc[50,0])
```
